claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has moderate hardness and strength together with favorable ductility.
Titanium promotes local chemical short-range order in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti-induced chemical short-range order lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy favors partial-dislocation slip and transient stacking-fault formation over full-dislocation pile-up.
Partial-dislocation slip and transient stacking faults enable easier plastic deformation and moderate work hardening.
The proposed mechanism reduces work hardening relative to Ti-containing high-entropy alloys that develop brittle intermetallics.
The starting equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a homogenized, single-phase solid solution with minimal grain-boundary effects.
Ti-induced local chemical fluctuations affect dislocation-core structures.
Dislocation slip can control plastic deformation, with deformation degree related to dislocation density.
Previous CoCrFeNi-based systems showed a correlation between mechanical behavior and dislocation motion.
Partial-dislocation activity and transient stacking faults will be pronounced in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
Reducing Ti content or altering processing will disrupt the expected chemical short-range order.
A reduced-Ti or CSRO-disrupted variant should have higher hardness and strength with reduced ductility.
A reduced-Ti or CSRO-disrupted variant may deform by full-dislocation glide rather than the proposed partial-dislocation mechanism.
Composition changes can produce large changes in strength, work hardening, and ductility.
High-temperature precipitation, particularly at grain boundaries, can reduce alloy plasticity.
